newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: INTERVIEW - Venezuelan Sudamtex sees July-Dec net up.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Venezuelan Sudamtex sees July-Dec net up.

text.p: Despite a severe domestic recession, Venezuelan textiles and fibreglass manufacturer Sudamtex expects first half net profits for fiscal 1997 to rise five percent in real terms on the year before, company President Kenneth Johnson told Reuters.

"Total sales will probably be between flat and up three percent with exports compensating for lower local sales. But net income should be up some five percent on better margins," he said. The first half of the company's fiscal year is from July to December.

Venezuela's second largest private sector exporter reported year-end sales of 64 billion bolivars ($136 million) in June and net profits of eight billion bolivars ($17 million), all expressed in constant June 30 bolivars.
The improved margins largely derive from $100 million in production upgrades and plant investment, which only came fully on stream last year.
"We're probably now the most modern textile company in the whole of Latin America," said Johnson, who undertook the expansion with an eye towards taking advantage of greater regional integration.

With operations in both Uruguay and Venezuela -- as well as in Belgium and the UK where Sudamtex supplies retailing chain Marks & Spencer -- "We're really pushing for greater trade integration, especially Venezuela joining Mercosur."
Exports as a percentage of total sales have steadily risen, reaching 60 percent in 1996 from 57 percent in 1995.

In addition, Korean industrial giant Samsung is expected to sign soon for an investment that will double Sudamtex's Uruguay operations. Samsung will pay for the expansion and take all the additional production for the first five years.
"The deal should be put to bed in the next 30 days," he said.

But while textiles have traditionally represented the 50- year-old company's core business, "You can't ignore that the most significant change in Venezuela over the past year has been the oil opening," Johnson said.

The company -- which has only turned a loss once, in 1981 -- has recently created a petroleum division designed to piggy-back on the sector's opening to foreign investment by providing fibreglass storage tanks and high-pressure tubing.
Fiscal 1997 sales of the energy equipment are expected to reach $17 million, rising to $50 million in three years, so that "over time textiles will contribute less and less to total sales".
The debt taken on to fuel recent investments "is manageable, given our cash flow," Johnson said.
Total group bank debt currently stands at some $100 million, but interest coverage, at 2.2 percent "is very strong," he added, and total exposure is only "around $10 million."
"We think next year will be a truly strong one with up to 5 percent growth," Johnson said.
